sources.notes: Downloaded PDF (22 PDF pages, 20 numbered slides); read through text extraction (pdftotext). PDF metadata author: Eric Schost, based on lecture notes by many other CS341 instructors; PDF creation date February 2026, which is not a publication year and no course term is stated, so year is null. Slide numbers are the footers (n / 20); slide 10 occupies two PDF pages. Read closely: slides 5 to 10 (BFS algorithm, runtime, correctness 1 and 2, summary and applications). Components and BFS-tree slides seen only as text lines, not read closely. Lecture slides, not peer reviewed; the connectivity step 'true iff all vertices are connected to s' is stated without proof.

claims.text: Breadth-first search from a start vertex s discovers a vertex v if and only if there is a walk from s to v. The lecture proves both directions: every discovered vertex has a walk from s (induction on the order of discovery), and every vertex with a walk from s is discovered (induction along the walk).

support.quote: For all vertices v, there is a walk s ; v in G if and only if discovered[v] is true at the end
For all vertices v, if discovered[v] is true at the end, there is a walk s ; v in G
For all vertices v, if there is a walk s ; v in G, discovered[v] is true at the end

claims.text: The same lecture lists testing whether G is connected as an application of BFS, with the condition that all vertices are connected to s; it gives no proof of that step.

support.quote: testing if G is connected (true iff all vertices are connected to s)

claims.text: For a simple undirected graph, G is connected if and only if BFS from any one vertex s discovers every vertex. Proof: connected gives a path from s to each v; conversely, walks s to u and s to v give a (u, v)-walk by reversing the first and appending the second, and a walk contains a path.

support.quote: For all vertices v, there is a walk s ; v in G if and only if discovered[v] is true at the end
there is a path from u to v of length ≤ k.

claims.derivation: modules/m3.md, section 3.7, proof of the connectivity step

claims.text: Connectivity test. For a simple graph with N >= 2 vertices the following are equivalent: (a) G is connected; (b) for every i different from j some (A^k)_ij with 1 <= k <= N - 1 is positive; (c) every off-diagonal entry of A + A^2 + ... + A^(N-1) is positive; (d) every entry of (I + A)^(N-1) is positive. Proved from walk counting (C16), walk contains path (C31, C33), path length bound (C35), nonnegativity of the entries, and the binomial theorem for I and A.

support.quote: Let G be a simple graph on [n], and let A be the adjacency matrix of G. Then G is connected if and only if all the entries of (In + A)n−1 are positive.
Then, AG is connected if and only if bij ≠ 0, when i ≠ j.
any path from u to v must have length ≤ n − 1, where n is the number of vertices of G

claims.text: Restatement of m2 Proposition 3 (claim C-m2-03, proved in m2; no second proof here): for vertices u, v of a simple graph the existence of a (u, v)-trail (the book's path, Def. 1.2.12), of a (u, v)-walk, and of a (u, v)-path with no repeated vertex (Def. 1.2.13) are equivalent, so textbook Definition 2.1.1 and the course convention define the same connected graphs. Used by m3 as Lemma E.

claims.text: For a simple graph with N >= 2 vertices, n_i and n_j lie in the same connectivity component if and only if the (i, j) entry of (I + A)^(N-1) is positive; the component of n_i is the set of n_j with a positive entry in row i.

claims.text: The textbook defines the relation alpha on V by u alpha v if and only if a (u, v)-path exists in G, and states that it is reflexive (v alpha v for every v), symmetric and transitive. Interpretation, consistent with m2's convention that a walk of length 0 is allowed (C-m2-06): the reflexivity is about the book's path relation and does not itself define walk length; the book is silent on k = 0 in Definition 1.2.10.

claims.text: With A as input, BFS reads at most N times N matrix entries, order N^2, because each vertex is dequeued at most once and each dequeue scans one row of N entries; the sum form of the test by naive matrix multiplication costs order N^3 per product and N - 2 products, order N^4. The slides' O(n + m) bound is for adjacency lists. Complexity is out of scope beyond this remark.

support.quote: each vertex is enqueued at most once

claims.text: On all labelled simple graphs with N = 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 vertices (2, 8, 64, 1024, 32768 graphs; 1, 4, 38, 728, 26704 connected) the sum test, the (I + A)^(N-1) test, a union-find check from the edge list, and (for N up to 5) explicit walk enumeration all agree, and the smallest k with a positive entry equals the BFS distance. Finite check, not a proof.

claims.text: Worked examples: for the board matrix (edges n1n2 and n2n3), A^2 has rows 1 0 1 / 0 2 0 / 1 0 1, B = A + A^2 has rows 1 1 1 / 1 2 1 / 1 1 1, (I + A)^2 has rows 2 2 1 / 2 3 2 / 1 2 2, all positive, connected. For the graph with the single edge n1n2, A^2 has rows 1 0 0 / 0 1 0 / 0 0 0, B has rows 1 1 0 / 1 1 0 / 0 0 0, (I + A)^2 has rows 2 2 0 / 2 2 0 / 0 0 1, so not connected, with components {n1, n2} and {n3}. A^2 alone has (A^2)_12 = 0 in the connected example, and for the path graph on N vertices the smallest k with (A^k)_(1,N) > 0 is N - 1 for N = 2..7.
